passages.text: For the writings took on many false statements against God for this reason: when the prophet Moses, by God’s counsel, had handed down the law together with its interpretations to some chosen persons, seventy in number, so that they too might equip those among the people who wished it, not long afterward, once the law had been put into writing, it took on some false statements against the sole God, who created heaven and earth and everything in them, because the evil one dared to bring this about for a certain just reason. And this happened with reason and judgment, so that it might be shown who dare eagerly to listen to the things written against God, and who, out of affection for him, dare not only to disbelieve the things said against him but even to refuse to tolerate hearing them at all, even if they should happen to be true, judging it much safer to take a risk for reverent faith than to live with a troubled conscience over blasphemous words.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes the authoritative written corpus under discussion without importing the boundaries or capitalization of a later canon.
γνώμη may mean judgment, purpose, decision, or counsel; “counsel” presents Moses’ transmission as occurring by divine determination.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some chosen persons, seventy in number
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves both the indefinite force of τισίν and the stated number without making “some seventy” sound approximate.
The phrase grammatically accompanies the evil one’s action. The difficult claim that his action occurred for a just reason is retained rather than reassigned to another agent.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ γραφέντα φιληκόως ἔχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: eagerly to listen to the things written against God
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιληκόως expresses fondness for hearing or eagerness to listen, contrasting with the following group’s refusal even to hear such statements.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνες τολμῶσιν τὰ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ γραφέντα φιληκόως ἔχειν τίνες τε στοργῇ τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸν τὰ κατ’ αὐτοῦ λεγόμενα μὴ μόνον ἀπιστεῖν, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀκούειν ἀνέχεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: who dare eagerly to listen to the things written against God, and who, out of affection for him, dare not only to disbelieve the things said against him but even to refuse to tolerate hearing them at all
lexical_decisions.rationale: The predicate τολμῶσιν governs both coordinated τίνες clauses. Repeating “dare” in English preserves the boldness attributed both to those who welcome the accusations and to those who reject them; “even to refuse” conveys the emphatic escalation of μηδὲ with the negative sense of ἀνέχεσθαι.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even if they should happen to be true
lexical_decisions.rationale: The antecedent is the things said against God. Greek permits the singular verb with the neuter plural predicate, and the author’s striking concession is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to take a risk for reverent faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὔφημος concerns favorable or reverent speech, in contrast with the blasphemous words that follow. An alternative is “to take a risk for faith that speaks well of God.”

source_issues.source_quote: κἂν ἀληθῆ τυγχάνῃ; πολλῷ κρίναντες ἀσφαλέστερον· περὶ εὐφήμου πίστεως κινδυνεύειν ἢ ἐπὶ βλασφήμοις λόγοις δυσσυνειδήτως βιοῦν.
source_issues.issue: The supplied punctuation places a question mark after τυγχάνῃ and a middle dot after ἀσφαλέστερον, although κρίναντες and the following comparative infinitives form a coherent continuation of the preceding description. The translation treats the punctuation as editorial and follows the grammatical connection without altering the supplied Greek wording.
